title: Shane Warne
wiki_lead:
Shane Keith Warne (13 September 1969 – 4 March 2022) was an Australian international cricketer whose career ran from 1992 to 2007. Warne played as a right-arm leg spin bowler and a lower-order right-handed batter for Victoria, Hampshire, the Melbourne Stars and Australia. Warne is regarded by many cricket players, statisticians and sporting analysts as not just the greatest ever leg spinner, but one of the greatest bowlers in the history of cricket. Warne also played for and coached the Rajasthan Royals, including captaining the team to victory in the inaugural season of the IPL.
He made 145 Test appearances, taking 708 wickets, and set the record for the most wickets taken by any bowler in Test cricket, a record he held until 2007. Warne was a useful lower-order batsman who scored more than 3,000 Test runs, with a highest score of 99. Warne was a member of the Australian team that won the 1999 Cricket World Cup. He retired from international cricket at the end of Australia's 2006–07 Ashes series victory over England.
Warne published his autobiography, No Spin, in 2018.
Warne revolutionised cricket thinking with his mastery of leg spin, then regarded as a dying art. After retirement, he regularly worked as a cricket commentator and for charities and endorsed commercial products. During his career, Warne was involved in off-field scandals including a ban from cricket for testing positive for a prohibited substance, a colourful personal life and interactions with gambling figures.
On 4 March 2022, Warne died of a heart attack at the age of 52, while on holiday in Thailand. After his death, many tributes and memorials were made to Warne, both in his home city of Melbourne and elsewhere in the cricketing world. Warne was posthumously appointed an Officer of the Order of Australia (AO) for his service to cricket.

Early life
Warne was born in Upper Ferntree Gully, Victoria, a suburb of Melbourne, on 13 September 1969, the son of Brigitte (née Szczepiak) and Keith Warne. His mother was born in Germany of a German mother and a Polish father who had migrated to Germany as a teenager.
According to his autobiography, when Warne was in kindergarten, another boy jumped on his back and broke both his legs. He used a trolley powered by his arms to get around for 12 months, which he credited for his wrist strength.
He attended Hampton High School from Grades 7–9 before being offered a sports scholarship to attend Mentone Grammar, where he spent his final three years of school.


Early career
Warne's first representative honours came in the 1983–84 season when he represented University of Melbourne Cricket Club in the Victorian Cricket Association's under-16 Dowling Shield competition. He bowled a mixture of leg-spin and off-spin, and was a handy lower-order batsman.

grok_lead: Shane Keith Warne (13 September 1969 â 4 March 2022) was an Australian international cricketer widely regarded as one of the greatest bowlers in the history of the sport and the greatest leg-spinner in cricket history, commonly referred to as the "King of Spin", "King of Leg Spin", "Leg Spin Wizard", "wizard" or "magician" of spin, and a cricketing legend. He played 145 Test matches and 194 One Day Internationals (ODIs) for Australia between 1992 and 2007, amassing a total of 1,001 international wickets, including a then-record 708 Test wickets at an average of 25.41. Warne's career highlights included his iconic "Ball of the Century" to dismiss England's Mike Gatting in the 1993 Ashes series, earning him Man of the Match in the 1999 Cricket World Cup final with figures of 4/33, and leading Australia to multiple series victories, particularly against England where he claimed 195 Ashes wickets. His innovative variations, such as the googly, flipper, and slider, combined with his competitive mindset, made him a pivotal figure in Australia's dominant era, contributing to their retention of the Ashes in 2006â07 as he retired with 23 wickets in that series alone. Born in Ferntree Gully, Victoria, Warne made his first-class debut for Victoria in 1991, following a release from the Australian Cricket Academy in 1990 due to disciplinary issues. His Test debut came against India in Sydney in January 1992, where he took 1/150 and 2/78, but it was his rapid rise thereafter that defined his legacy: by 1993, he had engineered Australia's Ashes triumph with 34 wickets, including the legendary delivery that drifted and spun sharply to bowl Gatting. Warne achieved numerous milestones, such as becoming the first bowler to take 100 Test wickets in a foreign country ( England, 2005), surpassing Dennis Lillee's Australian record of 355 Test wickets in 2000, and briefly holding the world record for most Test wickets in 2004 before being overtaken by Muttiah Muralitharan. He recorded 37 five-wicket hauls in Testsâthe most by any bowler at the timeâand was named one of Wisden's Five Cricketers of the Twentieth Century in 2000, alongside legends like Don Bradman. Warne's career was not without controversy, marked by off-field indiscretions that often overshadowed his on-field brilliance. In 1995, he and teammate Mark Waugh were fined for providing pitch and weather information to an Indian bookmaker during a tour of Sri Lanka, a scandal that highlighted early concerns over match-fixing in cricket. More severely, in 2003, Warne received a 12-month ban from Cricket Australia after testing positive for a banned diuretic ahead of the World Cup, which he claimed was used for weight loss but led to his exclusion from the tournament. His personal life drew tabloid attention through repeated sex scandal s, including lewd phone calls to a British nurse in 2000 and a leaked video in 2006 showing him in compromising situations, which he attributed to his impulsive nature but which strained his marriage and public image. Despite these, Warne's charisma and resilience endeared him to fans, and he captained Australia in 11 ODIs with a strong win rate. After retiring from international cricket following the 2006â07 Ashes, Warne continued playing in domestic and Twenty20 leagues, notably captaining the Rajasthan Royals to victory in the inaugural Indian Premier League (IPL) in 2008, where his tactical acumen shone. He later coached and mentored young spinners while pursuing interests in professional poker, authoring books like his 2001 autobiography Shane Warne's Comeback, and appearing in media. In retirement, Warne became a prominent commentator for Fox Sports in Australia, offering sharp insights on spin bowling and tactics until his death. Tragically, Warne died of natural causesâa heart attackâon 4 March 2022 while on holiday in Koh Samui, Thailand, at age 52; he had reportedly been on a 14-day liquid diet for weight loss prior to the incident. His passing prompted global tributes, including a state memorial at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where a stand was renamed in his honor, cementing his legacy as the "King of Spin", "King of Leg Spin", "Leg Spin Wizard", and a cricketing legend.
